title: Demonstrate knowledge of the prerequisites for perishable produce export inspection

lessons.title: Legal requirements and food safety before inspection
lessons.html:
Legislative requirements and pre-inspection preparation

Before a PPECB inspector will assess a consignment for export, several legal and administrative conditions must already be met. If any are missing, the inspection cannot go ahead and the fruit may miss its vessel.

  • Registration: the exporter must be registered with PPECB, and the production unit (PUC) and packhouse (PHC) must be registered, including for any market that requires special registration.
  • Food business operator registration: role-players handling export produce must be registered as required by the regulations, so that each can be identified.
  • Export standards: the consignment must be packed according to the export standards and requirements under the Agricultural Product Standards Act 119 of 1990 for that product.
  • Market protocols: for markets with phytosanitary protocols, orchard pest monitoring and other conditions must have been met during the season.
  • Inspection request: the exporter or packhouse books the inspection in advance through the PPECB system, giving consignment details.

Mandatory food safety requirements

Food safety is a condition of export. The key mandatory requirements include:

  • Residue compliance: pesticide residues must be within the maximum residue limits of the destination market. Producers keep spray records and many exporters do residue tests before shipping.
  • Use of registered agricultural remedies under Act 36 of 1947, according to the label.
  • Hygiene: packhouses must maintain clean facilities, safe water, worker hygiene and pest control.
  • Traceability: every carton must be traceable to its producer and packhouse.

Practices that maintain these standards include a spray programme checked against market MRL lists, a hygiene management system in the packhouse, documented cleaning schedules, training of staff and internal audits. Private schemes such as GLOBALG.A.P. help farms organise and prove these practices.

lessons.title: Packaging, containers, traceability and marking
lessons.html:
Standards for packaging materials and containers

Export packaging must protect the fruit for a journey of several weeks in cold, humid conditions. The export standards and buyer specifications set requirements such as:

  • Strength: cartons must withstand stacking on pallets and high humidity without collapsing.
  • Ventilation: vent holes must line up when cartons are stacked so cold air can reach the fruit.
  • Cleanliness: packaging must be new or clean, stored off the floor and protected from pests, dust and chemicals.
  • Approved inner packaging: liners, trays, punnets, wraps and pads of the correct type.
  • Pallets: correct size and strength; wooden pallets and packaging may need treatment to meet international rules on wood packaging.
  • Containers and vessels: reefer containers and holds must be clean, odour-free, in good working order and pre-cooled where required, and approved by PPECB for the cargo.

Traceability systems

A traceability system lets anyone trace a carton backwards to its orchard and forwards to its buyer. It is required by law and by buyers, and it limits the damage if there is a problem: only the affected lots need to be recalled.

  • On the farm: each bin is linked to an orchard block (PUC), harvest date and picking team.
  • In the packhouse: bins are linked to packing runs; each carton and pallet gets codes and a pallet number or barcode.
  • In logistics: pallet numbers are linked to containers, vessels and shipping documents.

Marking requirements

Cartons must be marked as the export standards require. Typical markings include the product and cultivar, class, count or size, net mass where needed, the packer or exporter identification, the production unit code and packhouse code, the packing date or code, and the country of origin. Some markets require extra markings. Marking must be clear, correct and the same on every carton in a pallet.

lessons.title: Presenting a consignment for inspection
lessons.html:
What it means to present a consignment

Presenting a consignment means making it ready, available and correctly documented so that the inspector can do an accurate and efficient inspection. Poor presentation wastes the inspector's time, delays the shipment and can lead to failure for reasons that have nothing to do with fruit quality.

Preparation steps

  1. Book the inspection in time and confirm the consignment details: product, cultivar, class, market, number of pallets and cartons.
  2. Group the pallets of the consignment together in one area, ideally in the cold store or a cool inspection area, not spread around the packhouse.
  3. Make pallets accessible so cartons can be drawn from any pallet and position. Leave space for the inspector to move and handle pallets safely.
  4. Check marking and pallet cards: every pallet must have a pallet card or label with the right codes, and the cartons must match.
  5. Provide documents: the consignment note or inspection request, packing list, and any market-specific records such as orchard registration or treatment records.
  6. Prepare the inspection area: a clean, well-lit table, scales, and the facilities the inspector needs, at the correct temperature where possible.
  7. Have a responsible person available to assist and to receive the result.

During and after inspection

  • Do not interfere with the inspector's choice of sample.
  • Return or replace sample cartons according to the procedure.
  • If the consignment fails, isolate it and decide on re-work, downgrading or redirection, then re-present only if the rules allow.
  • Keep the inspection result with your records for traceability.

Key points

  • Exporter, production unit and packhouse must be registered before inspection.
  • Residues, registered remedies, hygiene and traceability are mandatory food safety requirements.
  • Packaging must be strong, ventilated, clean and approved.
  • Traceability links every carton to its orchard, packhouse and container.
  • Present the consignment grouped, accessible, correctly marked and documented.
